w: Before the gold rush this was grassy woodland along Bendigo Creek, a food and water source for the Dja Dja Wrung. Then came puddling mills and shafts, and a 66-acre Government Camp of gaol, law courts and gold office. In 1861 the camp was handed over for parkland instead - the layout planted since 1870 still holds.
s: A government gold camp, turned into a park
_facts: Before white settlement, grassy woodland around Bendigo Creek was a food and water source for the Dja Dja Wrung people
Gold discovered in the 1850s transformed the area with puddling mills, shafts and mine waste
In 1852 the area was designated a Government Camp precinct of 66 acres with police barracks, gaol, law courts and a gold office
In 1856 gold commissioner Joseph Panton first suggested turning the camp into a park
In 1861, 59 acres were formally reserved as parkland and handed to the Sandhurst Borough Council; first gardener appointed 1870, establishing the layout that remains today

w: Reed, Barnes and Tappin drew up the Gothic Revival design in 1895 for the Roman Catholic Diocese of Sandhurst, and Sacred Heart has served as its cathedral and the bishop's seat ever since. Heritage-listed on the Victorian register since 1997, it's Bendigo's grandest legacy of the gold-boom decades.
s: Gothic Revival seat of the Sandhurst diocese
_facts: Roman Catholic cathedral church of the Diocese of Sandhurst and seat of the Bishop of Sandhurst, in Bendigo, Victoria
Designed in Gothic Revival style in 1895 by an architect of the firm Reed, Barnes and Tappin
Listed on the Victorian Heritage Register on 4 September 1997

w: One of Australia's oldest and largest regional art galleries, still run by the City of Greater Bendigo. No flashy backstory here - just a rare civic institution for a city its size, built on the same gold-boom wealth that raised Bendigo's cathedrals and parks.
s: One of Australia's oldest regional galleries
_facts: One of the oldest and largest regional art galleries in Australia
Owned and managed by the City of Greater Bendigo
